# Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment: The Industrial-Services Unit

Two restructurings that cut costs but not losses are not two failures — they are one diagnosis delivered twice. The problem was never the cost base. Cost cuts treat the denominator of a service business while the numerator — orders, price, utilization — keeps falling. Worse, in field services the people you cut *are* the revenue capacity, so each round of cuts accelerates the decline it was meant to fix.

> **The governing rule: the unit is not the unit of analysis.** A loss-making average hides profitable cells (customer × service line × contract). The real questions are: *Is there a profitable core inside this unit? Can we execute its turnaround in twelve months? And is the group even the right owner of it?* Everything below runs in service of those three questions.

---

## 1. First Read: What the Four Symptoms Already Say

Before any new analysis, the evidence pattern is unusually informative:

| Symptom | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Losses persist after two cost restructurings | The disease is revenue, price, mix, or contract quality — not cost. Salami-slicing headcount twice probably cut field and sales capacity, worsening response times and order intake. |
| Shrinking order book | Either the served market is declining (structural) or share is being lost (execution/position). The diagnostic must separate these — they have opposite prescriptions. |
| Best managers transferring out | Talent votes with its feet first. The group is strip-mining the unit through its own internal mobility policy — a **governance problem**, not a labor-market problem. It also means remaining leadership may be too weak to execute a turnaround without intervention. |
| Shared customers with profitable divisions | Two implications: (a) the stated loss may be partly a **transfer-pricing artifact** — the unit may service group equipment or shared accounts at negotiated-down internal prices, with the real profit sitting in the product divisions' P&Ls; (b) exit is entangled — shutting down service could hand competitors a Trojan horse into the group's most profitable accounts. |

**The likely mechanism — a service death spiral:** cuts → response times slip → key accounts defect → technician utilization falls → unit costs *rise* → losses persist despite cuts → morale falls → best people transfer out → service quality slips further. You break this loop at utilization, pricing, and talent — not at headcount.

**Working hypothesis (to be confirmed or killed in six weeks):** the losses are predominantly **execution- and governance-driven, with structural pockets** — a profitable installed-base core being dragged under by a loss-making project tail, mispriced legacy contracts, and internal pricing distortion. But three years of decline may have let structural erosion set in; that is what the diagnostic must test.

---

## 2. The Diagnostic: Structural or Execution? (Weeks 0–6)

Three tests, run in parallel, at cell level — not unit level.

**Test 1 — The pool test (is the market structural?).** Size and growth of each served segment; competitor results in the same segments. *If competitors serving the same customers are profitable and growing, the losses are not structural at market level — they are share and execution.* If the whole pool is shrinking or the basis of competition has shifted (OEMs in-sourcing service, remote monitoring displacing field labor, procurement consolidating to national players), it's structural.

**Test 2 — The position test (is our disadvantage structural?).** Within growing pools, do we hold advantage: installed-base access (especially the group's own equipment), certifications, geographic density, response-time capability? Subscale footprint in a density-driven business is a structural disadvantage no manager can outrun.

**Test 3 — The economics restatement (is the P&L even real?).** Rebuild the P&L three ways:
- **Contract margin census** — every contract, fully costed. Expect the bottom 10–20% of contracts to destroy more than 100% of the total

run.userPrompt:
A diversified group's industrial-services unit has lost money for three straight years despite two restructuring attempts that cut costs but not losses. The unit serves some customers who also buy from the group's profitable divisions, its order book is shrinking, and its best managers keep transferring out. The board has given leadership one final year to produce a credible path to profitability or exit.

Produce the turnaround-or-exit assessment and plan. Diagnose whether the losses are structural or execution-driven, identify which customer segments and service lines could sustain profit, design the turnaround plan with milestones for the one-year deadline, and define the exit alternatives and the criteria for choosing between turnaround and divestment.
